nodes.question: What key principles of a wellbeing economy were respondents asked to rank in the study?
nodes.answer: Respondents were asked to rank dignity, nature and climate, social connection, fairness, and participation, along with two traditional economic indicators: economic growth and economic prosperity.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Objective As societies emerge from the COVID-19 pandemic, governments are increasingly moving away from a focus on economic growth at any cost towards the principles of a wellbeing economy, focused on achieving a more equitable distri- bution of wealth and wellbeing. This study aimed to assess the relative importance to the Australian general public of the key principles of a wellbeing economy and to investigate heterogeneity in preferences between demographic subgroups. Methods An online survey was developed and delivered to a general public sample of 2042 Australian adults (aged 18 years and above). Respondents were invited to rank the key principles of a wellbeing economy (dignity, nature and climate, social connection, fairness and participation) plus two additional traditional economic indicators of societal success ( economic growth and economic prosperity ) in order of their relative importance for informing future policy directions. Data analysis was conducted using simple summative scoring, which involved the use of a point system allocated to rankings as a depend- ent variable. In addition, a rank-ordered logit model was used to explore preferences for the entire sample and subgroups defined by key socio-demographic characteristics.

nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: Did the findings suggest a shift in government focus regarding societal success?
nodes.answer: Yes, the findings suggest that the public is likely to support a shift from traditional economic indicators to broader wellbeing economy measures of societal success.
nodes.paragraph: Results Dignity (people have enough to live in comfort, safety and happiness) and fairness (equal opportunity for all Australians and the gap between richest and poorest greatly reduced) were ranked as the most important priorities for the total sample and for key socio-demographic subgroups differentiated by age, level of education and level of socio-economic advantage. Traditional economic indicators of societal success including economic prosperity and economic growth were considered important but generally ranked below the principles of dignity and fairness Conclusions The findings indicate that government movements away from traditional economic indicators and towards new broader wellbeing economy measures of societal success are likely to be supported by the general public. * Rachel Milte rachel.milte@flinders.edu.au Matthew Crocker matthew.crocker@flinders.edu.au Gang Chen gang.chen@monash.edu Gordon Duff g.duff@unsw.edu.au Julie Ratcliffe julie.ratcliffe@flinders.edu.au 1 Health and Social Care Economics Group, Caring Futures Institute, Flinders University, Adelaide, GPO Box 2100, Adelaide, SA 5001, Australia 2 Centre for Health Economics, Monash University, Caulfield East, Melbourne, VIC 3145, Australia 3 Public Service Research Group, UNSW Canberra, Canberra, ACT 2600, AustraliaKey Points for Decision Makers The principles of dignity and fairness were the two most important priorities identified by Australians to guide policy in our survey conducted during the corona- virus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic.

nodes.question: What are some key principles that form the foundation of a wellbeing economy according to the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The key principles include dignity, nature and climate, social connection, fairness, and participation.
nodes.paragraph: Governments who are part of the WEAII acknowledge the role of economic growth and wealth creation as one potential indicator of collective wellbe - ing. However, they also acknowledge the importance of several other key principles which form the foundations of a wellbeing economy. These include: dignity everyone has enough to ensure that they can live in comfort, safety and happiness; nature and climate a restored and safe natural world for all life; social connection sense of belonging and institutions that serve the common good; fairness justice in all its dimensions is at the heart of economic systems and the gap between the richest and poorest in society is reduced and participation citizens are actively encouraged to engage in their communities and local economies [1 ]. The Federal Government of Australia has recently moved policy direction to align itself with the principles of a well- being economy through the announcement of a wellbe- ing budget [7 , 8]. Australia S first wellbeing budget was delivered in October 2022; it not only projected traditional measures of employment, gross domestic product (GDP) and national debt but also included measures of health and education outcomes, environmental sustainability, social inclusion and inequality for the first time [9 ].

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What were respondents asked to rank in the survey?
nodes.answer: Respondents were asked to rank key principles of a wellbeing economy (dignity, nature and climate, social connection, fairness, and participation) and two traditional economic indicators of societal success (economic growth and economic prosperity).
nodes.paragraph: The sam- ple was recruited purposively by Pureprofile (an Australian online research panel company with over 452,0 Austral- ian adults) to represent Australian population characteristics based on age group, gender and Australian state or territory of residence. The survey was administered at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, between September and Decem- ber 2020. Survey respondents were invited to complete a prefer - ence ranking exercise where they were asked to rank the key principles of a wellbeing economy (dignity, nature and climate, social connection, fairness and participation: Fig. 1) and two additional traditional economic indicators of soci- etal success ( economic growth , defined as an increase in the amount of goods and services produced in Australia and economic prosperity defined as full employment and low inflation rates). The survey also collected key socio-demo- graphic information including age, gender, level of income, employment status, highest level of education obtained and residential postcode. The collection of socio-demographic information facilitated an investigation of the potential for heterogeneity in ranking preferences in relation to these key principles between demographic subgroups. nodes.answer: Social sustainability encompasses health, influence, competence, impartiality, and meaning-making.

Sustainable practices aim to reduce our ecological foot - print and safeguard natural resources(Chakraborty and Thakur 2019 ; Galli et al. 2015 ; Gonzalez-Redin et al. 2024 ; Wiedmann and Barrett 2010 ). Meanwhile, the economic aspect of sustainability remains a topic of debate(Wilson 2023 ). Scholars discuss weak and strong sustainability, recognizing the importance of economic growth while seeking ways to decouple it from environ - mental harm(Hediger 2006 ; Islar et al. 2024 ; Neumayer 2013 ). This involves using fewer resources per unit of output while still promoting overall development. Lastly, social sustainability ensures that people do not encounter structural barriers(Ki jer and Langergaard 2023 ; Miller 2023 ). It encompasses health, influence, competence, impartiality, and meaning-making(Wolff and Ehrstr m 2020 ). Emphasizing equity, social justice, and community well-being, social sustainability contrib - utes to a holistic vision of a sustainable world(Amster 2020 ; Husgafvel 2021 ; Partridge 2014 ; ilenskyt et al. 2024 ).

nodes.question: What is the significance of radical social transformation in a resource-scarce world?
nodes.answer: In a resource-scarce world, radical social transformation is crucial to ensure the long-term sustainability of our economic and social systems.
